en: I learned the Creator had made it strong:
It has a fortified city around it.
Of radiant Beijing,
Within every one of its cities
There is also a carpeted garden!
Every kind of blessing
Was spread throughout broad Beijing;
Until the end of the age,
No one shall lay a claw upon it—
Almighty Allah, the one God,
Created it with this promise!
Great Beijing, blessed as paradise—
Can a man conquer it in war?
Look at its multitudes, like black worms!
Esteemed Beijing, land of the Kakanchin,
No mortal man has seen the whole of it;
Gracious Allah created
That teeming nation!
As I have heard from learned tradition,
The Flood's surging waters did not reach it;
Though slaughter lasted ninety years,
Its sacred power did not depart!
Its people were not routed and scattered;
Though famine lasted ninety years,
Its people's bellies did not hunger!
The land you face is Beijing;
My hero, my prince, heed my words.
You have taken the road to a stronghold,
Loading provisions on the finest tulpar!
Let us grieve and suffer;
Though I am a woman, stay awhile,
And let us say all we have to say!
My prince, if you go to Beijing, you will die;
When will you see this wretched woman again?
If you go to Kakan, you will die;
When will you turn and come back,
To the lady who cherishes you—
When will you see his face again?!
If the moon is covered in darkness,
What will become of the night?!
If, by chance, amid the shooting,
If, by mischance, amid the struggle,
You fail to return,
What will become of the days
Of wretched me, Aichürök?!
Without ill words, there are no good ones;
Without madness, there is no shaman.
Do not begin turmoil in Beijing;
My leopard, greater than other men,
Do not abandon your poor wife!
If you go to Beijing, take me with you;
When you reach the appointed place,
Slaughter disgraced, wretched me
There as a sacrifice!
Dig my grave broad,
And do not make me suffer hell while alive;
With your own hands, my gray wolf,
Place this disgraced, fierce woman
In that appointed place!
If, by chance, you pass away,
The black-cheeked battle-axe—
Who will mount it without letting it droop?
If Kyrgyz and Argyn remain,
Who will lead them without wreaking havoc?!
The battle-axe with a hawthorn haft—
Who will mount it without letting it whirl?
The surging Argyn and Kyrgyz—
Who will lead them without scattering them?!
If the journey lasts six months,
The tulpar’s head will turn to brain;
Among the many Argyn and Kyrgyz people,
Which one will come to be their master?!
You have prepared your stallion for Kakan,
And made great preparations to depart,
Leaving your Argyn and Kyrgyz people
Thus abandoned and desolate!
Your journey has become a distant one;
Your news may come from death!”
Having spoken such dreadful words,
Aichürök went openly
Before your gray wolf.
Swaying like a silk cushion,
Speaking with a tinkling laugh,
The white reins tied in a loop—
The wretched woman stepped playfully
And snatched them from his hand.
Twining herself in the reins,
She remained screaming and weeping;
Wrapping herself in the stirrup-leather,
She wept without restraint.
From the wretched woman’s singularly fair face,
White as the risen moon,
Tears now flowed untouched;
From her white face lit as by the sun,
Tears flowed as dusk gathered.
She sobbed in grief and wept,
Turning aside, she screamed and wept,
Saying, “When you reconnoiter Beijing, you will see;
When will you return to your poor wife?”
“Beijing is six months distant—
Take heed and do not call the road easy;
The Chinese people bring mighty suffering,
Do not despise them as weaker than men!
Beijing is five months distant—
Do not call its passes a short road;
Do not despise the restless Black Chinese
As inferior to other men!
Your opponent is the Kakanchin;
Without ill words there are no good ones.
If the moon is veiled in darkness,
What shall we do with the night?!
If death arrives and your days are done,
With no male child left behind,
What shall we do with our days?!
On the hard road toward Beijing,
You have chosen to ride on campaign,
And scattered your inexhaustible treasure
Across the open steppe!
Toward Beijing, the land of no return,
You have ridden out to begin reconnaissance!
You had need of wretched me,
Yet have abandoned your wife in desolation!”
Speaking thus, Aichürök
Screamed and cried aloud,
Sobbing in true grief.
The bones of her ribs seemed to split,
Her heart was grievously torn,
And tears poured from her eyes;
Unable to find her bearings,
The hair down her back grew thin.
Tears streaming from both cheeks
Poured down over her breast.
When she spoke, her words tasted of sugar;
Her black eyes shone like the morning star,
Yet tears flowed from both together.
From her dear eyes, like black currants,
Tears fell a whip’s length.
Her back seemed broken,
And in the wretched woman, radiant beyond mortals,
The form of a holy seer appeared.
The peerless Lady Chürök,
Of that infidel’s surpassing wisdom,
Stood barring the prince’s way.
Her waist a handful, her face like the moon,
What a renowned beauty,
The wretched daughter of the peri!
She turned Buurul’s head.
Twining herself in the reins,
She stood screaming and weeping;
Wrapping herself in the stirrup-leather,
She stood weeping inconsolably.
The splendid hero, born to surpass
His father, gray-wolf Manas—
Could he remain without going to Beijing?
The leopard’s very image—
Could he rest without going to Kakan?
The peerless, broad-chested warrior,
Great in courage and heedless,
Gave no thought at all
To whether he might die today.
Your gray wolf swelled with spirit,
He thundered aloud,
And spoke to Aichürök:
“One of the seven days is death;
Does one prosper by fearing death?
Are there people who never die?!
When the Almighty issues the decree,
When Azrael, who draws out souls,
Stretches forth his five fingers,
The cunning tongue that spoke is stilled;
In this deceitful world,
When death truly comes,
Who can flee and escape?!
Will the dug grave not take us in?
Will the black earth not swallow us!
To know every art,
You have become a saint, poor woman!
You have taken to weeping mightily,
Since you find weeping so delightful;
May your father Akun Khan die,
And your brothers Azhybai and Tümönbai
Die along with him!
May your princely father Akun Khan die;
If you delight so much in weeping,
May all your kin die!
Hear the ceaseless words
Of this ill-fated, fierce woman!
The road of holy war is a great road—
Is it right for a wife to bar it?
The Kakanchin is the foe I shall meet;
When I set out upon the holy campaign,
Can a wife bar my way?!
If this weeping is so fine,
May your father Akun Khan die.
If you weep in grief,
May all those you love die!
You have gone mad, poor woman;
Should a raider not take the road,
And should a woman not remain at home?
Look at the deeds of this shameless woman:
Should the sorrowing warrior not scout,
And should the wife not remain at home!
If she sits weeping over a patrol,
Will dark misfortune not overwhelm me?!
Release my hand, fierce woman;
Do not bar my road!
Is it right for the son of a true noble
To live without pursuing the blood-price?
The road of a campaign is precious and great;
When a wife sits weeping,
Can there be anything so splendid?!”
His face darkened and grew grim,
His violent rage rose fiercely;
His eyes blazed like a lion’s,
And bloodlust truly seized him.
The black-cheeked rawhide whip—
Its blow would deafen the ears—
He seized and swung,
And with a resounding crack struck Chürök,
Sending the blow across her flank!
Her fine silk shirt
Split along its folds;
From the poor woman, whose flesh was white as snow,
Blood welled and poured.
Her silk-brocade shirt
Split along its folds;
From the wretched daughter of the peri,
Blood welled and poured.
Screaming and crying aloud,
She let go of the reins,
And, sobbing, cursed the prince:
“You would not heed me when I said, ‘Do not go’—
May you never return from where you go!
Then, my sovereign,
May you never see your market-home again!
May you never return once you leave;
May you never see your caravan-home again!
Did I burn what was precious to you,
That you should stretch out and lash me?
Did I provoke your anger,
That you should beat me so brutally?!
Did I burn your treasured possession,
That you should strike me screaming,
And do this wondrous deed?
Had I stirred your rage before?!
You dug my grave deep;
Despising me as a mere woman, you beat me
And brought this marvel upon my head!
My sorrowful prince, be damned;
You were the one who stretched out and struck,
And I became the hide you stretched!”
Turning away and walking, she sobbed;
Semetey’s Aichürök—
The peerless servant woman, rich in wisdom—
Entered the palace screaming.
Driving them all swiftly without looking back,
